narrative:
The model determined that you have an 88.3% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the strongest influence, both pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile for grades in both Year 1 and Year 3, far below the average of roughly the 6th decile among students who were accepted. These consistently low academic standings in law school were the main reasons the model saw a high risk of bar exam failure.

Your LSAT score of 32 was the third most influential factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure, though less dramatically. It sits noticeably below the 37.2 average of accepted students.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.10, family income in the lower-middle bracket, full-time study plans, gender, and race played little or no role in the outcome. The system focused almost entirely on your law school performance and entrance exam score.

To improve your chances, you should consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score and, if possible, strengthening your academic record through additional coursework or a graduate program that demonstrates higher performance. These steps would directly address the factors that most hurt your current prediction. (218 words)
